metadata.title: Reflections
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: How a hidden map makes a reflection in Godot
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation; Godot 4.7.2 runs on Apple M4 Pro (evidence/planning-checks); see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Reflections. Learn how a shader can read a hidden map of the water, and use it to give a character a reflection that shows only over water.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Most people think a reflection means drawing the scene a second time. You do draw the character twice. But the hard part is knowing where the water is, and a shader can learn that from a map.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. The screen texture is a picture of what has been drawn so far, which a shader can read. Draw order says which things are drawn first. A label map is a layer of flat colors, each color a label. And a reflection is a flipped, fainter copy, seen in water.

terms.meaning: a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn
a copy of the screen made at one moment, which a shader can read
what is drawn first; later things cover earlier ones
a layer of flat colors, each color a label
a flipped, fainter copy seen in water

beats.narration_text: Watch the reflection. The character walks along the shore, and its reflection follows in the water. Over the sandbar, the reflection disappears. No script decides that. A shader looks up a map the player never sees.

A real Godot render in a framed window on the cream stage: the teal blob walks along the shoreline from left to right and its flipped reflection follows in the water, thins out over the sandbar until it is gone, and returns on the far side. Readouts 'over water' and 'over sand'.

beats.narration_text: A shader works one pixel at a time. For each pixel of the reflection, it has to decide: show this pixel, or hide it. To decide, it needs one fact. Is there water under me?

shot.visual_intent: A framed flat picture of the pond (grass band, water, sand spit, teal blob with its reflection area under it). Over the reflection area a grid of 8 by 6 cells appears (the pixel grid); a terracotta dot visits the cells one by one asking 'water?'; each cell then fills teal (show) where it lies over water and stays empty (hide) where it lies over the sand. Label 'show or hide?'.

show.event: picture and the empty pixel grid
cells over water filled, cells over sand empty

shot.motion_claim: A dot visits cell after cell and each answer decides the cell: teal where yes, empty where no.

beats.narration_text: Here is that fact, drawn as a map. Water is red. The coast is green. Everything else is left empty. Each flat color is a label, so this picture is a label map.

Labels land in turn: 'water' on the red, 'coast' on the green ring (with one terracotta ring around the ring), 'empty' on the bare stage.

beats.narration_text: You could hand this map to the shader as an ordinary texture. Then, for every pixel, you must work out where it sits on the map, whatever the camera is doing. The screen is already lined up with every pixel.

shot.visual_intent: Two panels on the cream stage. Right, 'the screen': the same pixel with one straight arrow to the same spot in a screen-sized copy, no box. A small label 'texture: an image a shader can read'.

beats.narration_text: There is one problem. Draw the map over the game, and the player sees a red and green sea. The shader should read the map. Nobody else should.

beats.narration_text: The fix is draw order. A game paints in layers, and later layers cover earlier ones. Paint the map first and the art second, and the art covers it. The player sees only the art.

shot.visual_intent: An isometric stack on the cream stage, three flat slabs landing one after another: 'map' (red and green) first, then 'art' (the pond picture), then 'character' (the teal blob). Beside the stack a top-down thumbnail updates after each slab: after the map, red and green; after the art, only the pond (the red and green gone); after the character, the pond with the blob. Label 'later covers earlier'.

shot.motion_claim: The art slab lowers onto the map slab and the thumbnail's red and green vanish.

beats.narration_text: A shader reads the screen texture: a copy of the screen made at one moment. Make it after the art, and the map is gone. Make it before the art, and the map is still in it.

beats.narration_text: Godot has a node for choosing that moment: Back Buffer Copy. It makes its copy at its own place in the draw order.

shot.visual_intent: The slab stack with a node chip labelled 'BackBufferCopy' sliding in between the map slab and the art slab; the copy frame snaps onto the chip and its thumbnail shows the map. A one-line label from the docs: 'copies the screen for a shader to read'.

beats.narration_text: And the draw order is the scene tree. The top of the Scene dock is drawn first. So the order is: map, copy node, art, character, reflection.

beats.act: II · When the Screen Is Copied
beats.narration_text: By default, Godot makes that copy the first time a shader asks for it, right before that shader's node is drawn. So the shader sees everything drawn before it, and nothing after.

shot.visual_intent: A stack of three flat sprites A, B, C (the act's three colours) with a window-shaped 'shader' chip hovering above. As the chip drops toward the stack a copy frame appears automatically right under the chip and captures A, B and C; a thumbnail shows all three. Caption 'the first shader that reads the screen triggers the copy'.

thumbnail shows A, B, C; caption settles

shot.motion_claim: The shader chip drops toward the stack and, just before it lands, a copy frame appears under it and captures A, B and C.

beats.act: II · When the Screen Is Copied
beats.narration_text: Tree order is not the only lever. Z index and canvas layers change the draw order too, and the copy follows them. But a copy only serves shaders on its own canvas layer.

shot.visual_intent: Three transparent sheets stacked in isometric view, labelled 'layer -1', 'layer 0', 'layer 1' (a small note 'a CanvasLayer node'). On layer -1 the map; on layer 0 the copy node, the art and the reflection (a window chip); on layer 1 a second window chip. A glowing arrow runs from the copy node to the reflection on its own sheet; an arrow toward the chip on layer 1 stops at the sheet edge with a cross. A side chip 'z index' reorders items inside one sheet.

beats.act: II · When the Screen Is Copied
beats.narration_text: Back Buffer Copy has three modes. Viewport copies the whole screen. Rect copies only a box. Disabled copies nothing, so Godot falls back to its automatic copy.

shot.visual_intent: The real Godot 4.7 BackBufferCopy class page in a browser window; the camera pushes in on the three CopyMode constants (Disabled, Rect, Viewport) with their one-line descriptions and one terracotta ring marks the list. The ring box is a placeholder: set it from the real capture.

beats.act: II · When the Screen Is Copied
beats.narration_text: A new Back Buffer Copy starts in Rect mode. The box covers only a corner of the screen, wherever the node is. Outside it, the docs call the result undefined. Here the window reads black until the mode becomes Viewport.

shot.visual_intent: The three squares and the window, with the node in Rect mode at its defaults: the window is black except a tiny stage-coloured patch at its top-left corner (the only part copied). At 9 s the mode is switched to Viewport and the window fills with A, B and C. Readouts 'Rect mode' then 'Viewport'; one terracotta ring on the tiny patch.

lecture.runner_up: ShaderLab with the pond and the reflection
lecture.why: The black window shows 'undefined' literally and keeps this act's cast; the pond version is verified too but shows only a missing reflection.
lecture.capture_spec: C08: capture_scenes.gd id C08 (three squares and window; BackBufferCopy with copy_mode Rect at its default rect, node at (100,100); copy_mode set to Viewport at 9.0 s); 14.5 s planned, 30 fps, Forward+. MUST run in a fresh Godot process (the black needs an empty back buffer). 1:1 ROUTE, not the 4K route: a Rect box is measured in render pixels (run-13: on the 4K route the default box is only 34 canvas units), so capture_scene.sh renders C08 in the 1280 x 720 window itself, where the default box is the 100 px corner of the screen (run-10), and enlarges the frames 3x by whole pixels. The corner patch is 38 x 38 px in the window (0.578 to 0.608 of the frame's width, 0.078 to 0.131 of its height); the rect does not follow the node.

beats.narration_text: So the shader on the reflection looks up the same spot in the screen texture, using screen U V: a pixel's address on the whole screen. That texture holds the map, so the spot holds the label.

shot.visual_intent: Two linked panels of the pond: left 'the screen' with a terracotta dot on one pixel of the reflection, right 'the copy' (the red and green map) with its twin dot at the same place; a dashed link between the dots and the tag 'screen UV: the same address in both'. The dot moves along the reflection and its twin moves with it; the colour under the twin changes the small label from 'water' to 'sand' as the dot crosses onto the sandbar. A label 'screen UV: a pixel's address on the whole screen'.

beats.narration_text: The color it finds is the label. If it is close to red, this pixel is over water, so keep it. If not, set its alpha, how visible the pixel is, to zero.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the ten-line reflection shader); at right the real pond with the shader on the reflection: the blob walks, the reflection shows over water and is gone over the sandbar. The lines light up as the voice reads: the lookup line, the water test, the alpha line. Readouts 'keep' over water and 'alpha zero' near the sandbar.

cues.label: SCREEN_UV: a pixel's address on the whole screen
distance: how far apart two colors are
alpha: how visible a pixel is: 0 invisible, 1 solid

A small label '256 steps per channel' and a grey credit 'Apple M4 Pro · Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ and Compatibility read the same'.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A label map is a layer of flat colors, drawn first and covered by the art. A Back Buffer Copy makes the screen texture at its own place in the draw order. The reflection is a flipped copy that follows the character and shows only where the map says water. Compare map colors with a distance, never with equals. Paint the map in pure values: zero or full. Coast and tint polish the look, and the reflection shows the character only.

A Back Buffer Copy makes the screen texture at its own place in the draw order.
The reflection is a flipped copy that follows the character and shows only where the map says water.
Compare map colors with a distance, never with equals.
Paint the map in pure values: zero or full.
Coast and tint polish the look, and the reflection shows the character only.
